title: Phishing campaign uses last week's Microsoft 365 outage as bait
summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign, observed on 13 November 2026 across multiple sectors, that poses as Microsoft 365 service-health notices and claims messages held during a purported Exchange Online incident on 12 November will be deleted within 24 hours unless the user clicks 'RESTORE MESSAGES'. Subjects follow the pattern 'Outage – ' plus a random six-character string, with display names such as 'MSF Outage Notification' or 'AMZ Service Health'. Microsoft assesses it as likely credential phishing but has not confirmed credential capture or follow-on compromise. Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines the messages.
why: Real outages make fake outage notices believable, and this one followed a genuine Exchange Online incident. A user who entered credentials gives an attacker a path to mailbox access, inbox rules, internal phishing and business email compromise, so the clean-up is about accounts, not only mail.
todo: Do now: search mail telemetry for the sender domains, subject pattern and destination listed in Microsoft's post (Microsoft also publishes advanced hunting queries there), and purge delivered copies.

Identify users who clicked through. For anyone who may have entered credentials: reset the password, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, check MFA registrations, and review sign-ins, OAuth consents, inbox and forwarding rules and delegates.
Tell users that real Microsoft 365 service-health information lives in the admin center and that Microsoft does not send them to non-Microsoft sites to recover held mail.
Hardening: make sure Safe Links, Safe Attachments and zero-hour auto purge are on, and keep moving admins and high-risk users to phishing-resistant MFA.
